I feel happy to present otorhinolaryngological fraternity of the country, the first otorhino­laryngology 
(ENT) textbook, which is based on the new Competency-based Medical Education (CBME) ENT 
Curriculum 2019 for Indian Medical Graduate (IMG). It is developed and implemented by National 
Medical Commission (NMC) erstwhile Medical Council of India (MCI). This third edition of “Diseases of 
Ear, Nose and Throat” presents the knowledge of diseases of ear, nose and throat in a concise format. 
The didactic presentation will make this textbook attractive to the medical students, residents and 
practitioners. I am grateful to the students and teachers for their feedback on its first and second 
editions and that facilitated the development of this third edition.

content.text:
When I started working for this third edition, I knew that it would be a challenge to organize 
the content in the format of new medical curriculum for undergraduates in consonance with 
the changing health needs of the country. I have strived to maintain the international standards. The new Graduate Medical 
Education Regulations (GMR/GMER 2019) intends to take the IMG to provide health care to the evolving needs of the nation 
and the world. As the IMG is supposed to provide preventive, promotive, curative, palliative and holistic care to his patients, this 
edition has a section on community medicine. I have tried my best to enunciate clearly the competencies that students must 
be imparted.

content.text:
The thrust in GMER (2019) is on making medical education more learner-centric, patient-centric, gender sensitive, outcome-
oriented and environment appropriate. As the student should be able to effectively communicate with patients and their 
relatives, the textbook has a section on AETCOM (Attitude, Ethics and Communication). It gives me great satisfaction to state 
that this  “competency-based otorhinolaryngology undergraduate textbook” has been prepared keeping in mind the NMC/
MCI’s vision of creating a competent IMG to serve the community. Wherever felt necessary, the “broad subject competencies” 
have been split into “sub-competencies”. Keeping in mind the “patient centric curriculum”, case studies are incorporated in the 
chapters liberally. Even the first year students can read the Anatomy and Physiology of Ear, Nose, Throat, Head and Neck from 
this book because keeping in mind the “early clinical exposure”, plenty of case studies are given in the Anatomy and Physiology 
chapters.

content.text:
Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat with Head and Neck Surgery that represents otorhinolaryngology, head and neck surgery in 
all of its diversity, is created to fill the need of contemporary definitive book. The reader will find boxes, tables, flow charts, 
line diagrams and photographs, which serve to enhance learning. The book is comprehensive and of broader scope and 
is designed for students, residents and practitioners alike. It offers a balanced presentation of contents and emphasizes 
the practical features of clinical diagnosis and patient management. The students will like its simplicity, directness and 
clarity. Each chapter includes clear, compelling, and up-to-date discussions and expertly executed and generously sized art. 

The brevity, conciseness, readable format and easy accessibility of key information will facilitate efficient use in any practice 
setting. Each page is carefully laid out to place related text, figures, and tables near one another to minimize the need for page 
turning. To provide an overview, each chapter begins with the list of its contents (Points of Focus) and ends with a Further 
Reading section. Each chapter has a Clinical Highlights section for the quick revision of the students. This section has been 
especially prepared for answering frequently asked MCQs, short-answer questions and oral/viva questions. The Appendix 

contains Top 101 Clinical Secrets and Problem-oriented Cases which will be of immense use and interest to the readers.

content.text:
The new Graduate Medical Education Regulations 2019 (GMR/GMER 2019) intends to take the Indian Medical Graduate (IMG) 
in providing health care to the evolving needs of the nation and the world. The thrust is on making medical education more 
learner-centric, patient-centric, gender-sensitive, and outcome-oriented and environment appropriate. Emphasis is made on 
alignment and integration of subjects both horizontally and vertically. The end of phase subject (sub) competencies is mapped 
to the global competencies.

reasons: block type changes (heading_candidate -> paragraph)

content.text:
It attempts to provide the orientation and the skills necessary for life-long learning in IMG and that would enable proper care 
of the patient. The GMR 2019 reinforces skill acquisition aspect by necessitating certification of certain essential skills and suggests 
skill acquisition and assessment methods using skills labs, simulated and guided environments. Prior to the Internship the highest 
level of skill acquisition is a “Show How” (SH) in a simulated or guided environment. There is only one skill in ENT that requires 
independent performance and certification. Opportunity to ‘perform’ other skills would be made available during internship.

follicles, and ceruminous glands.

Otolithic membrane: The otoconial membrane 

The auditory pathway (Fig. 28) from peripheral to center 

consists of a gelatinous mass, a subgelatinous space 
consists of eighth nerve, cochlear nuclei, olivary complex 
and the crystals of calcium carbonate called otoliths 
(superior), lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial 
(otoconia or statoconia). The otoconia, which are 
multitude of small cylindrical and hexagonally shaped 
bodies with pointed ends, consists of an organic protein 
matrix together with crystallized calcium carbonate. 

The otoconia (3–19 µm long) lie on the top of the 
gelatinous mass. The cilia of hair cells project into the 
gelatinous layer. The linear, gravitational and head-tilt 
movements result into the displacement of otolithic 
membrane, which stimulate the hair cells lying in 
different planes.

content.text:

Respiratory mucosa: The respiratory mucous membrane, 
which covers the lower two-thirds of the nasal cavity, 
shows variable thickness. It is thickest over nasal conchae, 
especially at their ends. It is thick over the nasal septum and 
thin in the meatuses and floor of the nose. This respiratory 
mucous membrane is pseudostratified ciliated columnar 
epithelium and contains plenty of goblet cells. It is highly 
vascular and contains erectile tissue. The submucosal layer 
contains both racemose and tubular glands that secrete 
serous and mucous secretions for the surface mucous 
blanket. The deeper specialized vascular plexus (erectile 
tissue) consists of arterioles, capillaries, vascular sinusoids, 
venous plexuses and venules.

Ethmoidal sinuses are thin-walled air cavities in lateral masses 
of ethmoid bone. They vary in number (3–18) and lie between 
upper third of lateral nasal wall and the medial wall of orbit. 
Some of them are present at birth. Clinically, they are divided 
into two groups: (1) anterior and (2) posterior. Anterior ethmoid 
group opens into the middle meatus through several small 
openings under cover of middle turbinate. Posterior ethmoid 
group opens into the anterior part of superior meatus and 
some in sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior meatus.

(600–700 mL of nasal secretions in 24 hours), which form a

like a “conveyer belt” toward the nasopharynx. The complete 
sheet of mucous blanket reaches the pharynx in 10–20 minutes.

nucleus that is situated in the medulla. It then runs within the 
subarachnoid space and passes laterally across the posterior 
cranial fossa and exit the cranium via the hypoglossal canal.

hyoid bone) muscles. It then travels towards the angle of the 
mandible and crosses internal and external carotid arteries, 
and enter into the tongue. Another branch containing C1/C2 
fibers descends and joins ansa cervicalis that innervate the 
omohyoid, sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles, which all 
act to depress the hyoid bone.

content.text:
Pharynx is a 12–14 cm long conical tube which forms upper 
part of the air and food passages. It extends from basiocciput 
and basisphenoid to the lower border of cricoid cartilage. 
Inferiorly, it becomes continuous with the esophagus. 
Pharyngoesophageal junction (1.5 cm width) is the narrowest 
part of gastrointestinal tract apart from the appendix. The 
width of pharynx base, which faces toward skull base, is 
3.5 cm. Pharynx is traditionally divided into three parts: (1) 
nasopharynx, (2) oropharynx, and (3) hypopharynx.

content.raw:
This mobile and flexible palate forms the floor of nasopharynx 
and roof of the oropharynx. Anteriorly, it is attached to the hard 
palate and with the palatine aponeurosis. Its posterior border is 
free and has a central process (uvula) that hangs in the midline. 
The two arches bind it to the tongue and pharynx: the anterior 
tonsillar pillar (containing palatoglossal muscle) and posterior 
tonsillar pillar (containing palatopharyngeal muscle).Between 
these two pillars resides the tonsillar fossa in which lie the 
palatine tonsils (faucial tonsils).

posterior tongue. See Chapter 51 “Pharyngitis and Adenotonsillar

the base of arytenoid and a facet on the upper border of 
cricoid lamina. Two types of movements are possible at this 
joint; rotatory and gliding. The rotatory movement occurs 
at a vertical axis and abducts or adducts the vocal cord. 
Arytenoids glide laterally and medially and help in closing 
or opening the posterior part of glottis.

Glottis (Rima glottidis): This narrowest part of an adult 
laryngeal cavity lies between vocal cords and arytenoids 
of the two sides. Size and shape of glottis varies with the 
activities of the vocal cords. Anterior two-third of glottis 
is formed by membranous vocal cords while posterior 
one-third by vocal processes of arytenoids. Anteroposterior 
length of glottis is more in men (24 mm) than in women 
(16 mm).

A 40-year-man has right posterior toothache of lower jaw for the 
past 3 weeks. He was doing hot saline gargles for his problem. Now 
he develops fever and difficulty in opening the mouth (trismus)

examination, fever was recorded 102°F. On local examination, 
redness of the right submandibular region extending to the right

anxious and drooling saliva from the mouth. Mild inspiratory 
stridor (high-pitched whispering sound with respiration indicating 
obstruction of the airway) was also noted. His treating doctor says 
that mouth infection has spread to the neck and may eventually 
spread into the chest. See Chapter 52 “Abscesses in Relation to 
Pharynx (Deep Neck Infections)”.

Otorhinolaryngology (Oto: Ear; Rhino: Nose; Laryngo: Larynx-
Throat), which is also called as otolaryngology, is the specialty 
that deals with diseases of ear, nose, throat (ENT), head and neck 
region. Originally, the specialty was commonly called as EENT 
(eyes, ear, nose and throat) and included ophthalmology as 
well. But the two disciplines split many years ago because of the 
patience and practice because the examiner will have to deal with 

explosion of medical knowledge. In recent times, the specialty 
is usually called as ‘Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery’. 

The doctor who deals with the specialty is called ‘otolaryngo­
logist’/ear, nose, throat, head and neck surgeon.

Case Study 1
Vicky, a 35-year-old man, working as office superintendent, has 
been feeling a lump in his throat for the last 9 months. He feels as 
if something has stuck in his throat and points to the lower part of 
the front of his neck. These feelings are not continuous and occur 
off and on. Though as such there is no difficulty in swallowing food, 
however he feels sometimes difficulty in swallowing his own saliva. 
The severity of his complaint is neither decreasing nor increasing in 
the last 9 months. He does not have any associated history of throat 
pain, hoarseness of voice, neck swelling, fever or coughing. He is a 
teetotaler and does not give any history of smoking and chewing 
of Paan (specially prepared leave), Sopary (areca-nut) and tobacco. 
His lifestyle is sedentary but he is not suffering from diabetes or 
hypertension. He is afraid of cancer as his father, a chronic smoker 
died of cancer of throat a year ago. On examination, his general 
survey and local and systemic examination did not reveal any other 
abnormal findings. See Chapter 56 “Disorders of Esophagus”

and facial palsy are discussed in their respective chapters.

content.text:
Eustachian catheterization: Eustachian catheter, which 
is mainly used to test patency of the Eustachian tube 
is, sometimes, also helpful in removing FBs from the 
nose. After anesthetizing the nasal cavity with 4% 
lignocaine, Eustachian catheter is passed into the 
nasopharynx along the floor of nose. Then it is turned 
medially (90°) and slightly withdrawn till the posterior 
free border of the nasal septum is felt. Now it is rotated 
180° laterally to lie against the opening of Eustachian 
tube. A bulb is attached and then air is insufflated. An 
auscultation tube, which connects patient’s ear to that 
of the examiner, is employed. Hearing of the sound of 
air entering the middle ear indicates the patency of 
Eustachian tube.

content.text:
Case Study 1
In the monsoon season, a 40-year-old lady came to ENT OPD with 
the history of severe right ear pain and block (fullness/Hearing 
loss) feeling in right ear for 5 days. She is feeling some discharge 
in the right ear. She put some oil drops in the ear but that did not 
help rather she feels pain has increased after that and last night 
she could not sleep properly due to pain. On further inquiry, she 
admitted that 1 week ago she tried to clean her ear herself with 
hair pin. There is no history of cough and cold and fever. In the 
past, she has never suffered from such problem. She is not diabetic. 
On otoscopic examination, white plug dotted with black debris 
could be seen. There was no swelling of external ear canal and no 
ear discharge. Tympanic membrane was not visible. Rest of the 
local and general survey examination was normal. Rinne test was 
negative and Weber was lateralizing to right ear. See Chapter 33 
“Diseases of the External Ear”.

content.text:
Case Study 2
A 20-year-old girl has left ear discharge for 5 years. The discharge 
is thick, yellowish and putrid. She says discharge is continuous 
and never stops for more than couple of days or a week. She has 
used many ear drops but in vain. There is no history of ear pain, 
hearing loss, and vertigo or any other nose and throat problem. 
Patient does not have any headache, fever, or any swelling in 
the vicinity of left ear.  After the ear toilet, otoscopy examination 
was conducted. The posterosuperior deep retraction pocket with 
granulations and whitish flakes could be seen. Rest of the ear, nose 
and throat examination did not reveal any abnormality. Rinne test 
was negative and Weber was lateralizing to left ear.  The absolute 
bone conduction (ABC) test was normal. There was no nystagmus 
and fistula test was negative. See Chapter 35 “Chronic Suppurative 
Otitis Media and Cholesteatoma”.

Recruitment: Patients with recruitment have intolerance (increased sensitivity) to loud sounds. It is seen in cochlear

content.text:
Retrocochlear hearing loss: Lesions of cochlear nerve and nucleus will cause ipsilateral profound SNHL. A lesion at any 
other part of central hearing pathway (superior olive, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body, auditory 
radiations and primary auditory cortex in temporal lobe), which represent higher level of auditory processing, would result 
in mild bilateral hearing loss and decreased ability to localize a source of sound.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Weber test: External auditory canal obstruction and middle ear diseases cause CHL. The tuning fork (usually of 512 Hz) 
placed on the bridge of the nose or center of forehead will be heard better (lateralization) on the side of CHL. In Weber 
test, external and middle ears are bypassed. Air and bone conduction interfere with each other on the normal side, making 
that ear less sensitive.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Weber’s test lateralization: In external ear occlusion and middle ear diseases, Weber’s test will be lateralized toward 
the diseased ear. Right side lateralization denotes right ear CHL or left ear SNHL.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Rinne’s test: If Rinne’s test is negative with a TF of 512 Hz but positive for 1,024 Hz, minimum predicted A-B gap on 
audiometry would be 30 dB.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Gelle’s test: It examines the effect of increased air pressure in ear canal on the BC hearing. The TF is placed on the 
mastoid. The air pressure is increased in the EAC by Siegel’s speculum. Normally and in SNHL, increased middle ear 
pressure results in decreased hearing (Gelle’s positive). There is no change in hearing (Gelle’s negative) when ossicular 
chain is fixed (otosclerosis, tympanosclerosis) or disconnected usually (traumatic).

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss: With 512 Hz tuning fork, the Rinne’s test (without masking) may be false or 
negative but Weber’s test will be lateralized toward normal ear.

content.text:
Case Study
Manohar a 40-year-old male presented in ENT OPD with the history 
of hearing loss in both the ears for 5 years. The onset of hearing loss 
was so gradual that he does not remember how and when it started. 
So, he has gradually progressive painless hearing loss in both the 
ears. During working hours while talking with colleagues they 
had to shout as the hearing loss gets worsened in the presence of 
noisy background. He has been observing that loud sounds make 
him irritated. Now he finds difficulty in hearing even the normal 
conversation. He says “I can hear but cannot understand what the 
person is saying”. Sometimes, he has sensation of ear fullness and 
tinnitus and muffled hearing after the work. He does not give any 
history of dizziness, ear discharge, ear pain and headache.

He admitted that he had been smoking cigarettes for 20 years 
and did not get time for exercise. His diabetes and elevated blood 
pressure were diagnosed 2 years ago. He works in an industry

findings. Rinnes test was positive and Weber was not lateralize to 
any side. Absolute bone conduction test (ABC) was found reduced 
showing sensorineural hearing loss. See Chapter 36 “Sensorineural 
Hearing Loss”.

content.text:
Case Study
A middle aged man has been suffering from nasal obstruction for 
6 months. It started with an episode of common cold for which 
he was prescribed some medicines including nasal decongestant 
drops. He became much better with that treatment but continued 
nasal drops for the stuffiness of his nose. He feels obstruction of 
both sides of the nostrils. Nasal obstruction occurs on both sides 
of the nose simultaneously as well as on alternate side of the nose. 
In the morning after getting out of bed, he gets few sneezing and 
then rest of the day, there is no sneezing. His nasal obstruction is 
worst in night when he is sleeping and had to instill nasal drops 
for his nasal stuffiness. Now whenever he feels nasal obstruction 
he put nasal drops and frequency of putting nasal drops has been 
increasing. Sometimes, he gets clear thin nasal discharge from both 
or either side of the nose. There is no history of itching and episodes 
of sneezing. His problem of nasal obstruction becomes worst when 
he is exposed to direct flow of cold air of air conditioner, irritant 
fumes, and strong odor. His hypertension was diagnosed two 
year ago. General survey and local examination revealed nothing 
remarkable except the enlarged and congested turbinates on both 
sides of the nose. The nasal mucosa was boggy and edematous with 
clear mucoid secretions. Nasal septum was found not deviated.

See Chapter 44 “Vasomotor Rhinitis”.

content.text:
The development of cancer is a multistage process, which is 
usually painless to begin with. Therefore, the patients usually 
present at a very late and inoperable stages, which result in 
significant increase in morbidity and mortality. Early detection 
of malignancies can improve the compliance and follow up of 
these patients. An early cancer lesion may be missed as it may 
resemble to benign/premalignant lesion. The biggest challenge 
in early lesions is in deciding the site of biopsy. Following 
non-invasive OPD screening tools can facilitate in deciding the 
site of biopsy and in distinguishing cancers and premalignant 
lesions of oral cavity, pharynx and larynx early and offer chance 
of providing curative treatment. A proper clinical history and 
examination helps in distinguishing malignant lesions and the 
premalignant diseases (Table 1).

content.text:
Evaluation of throat is an integral part of ENT examination 
of children because it provides important clues or often the 
diagnosis per se. especially if the child has fever. Some of 
the common findings include follicles on the tonsils, quinsy, 
petechiae on the palate, congested throat, and mucosal ulcers.

reasons: block type changes (heading_candidate -> paragraph)

content.raw:
Although the basic principles of examining children are 
similar to adult, there are some important differences. The 
method of examination changes as a child develops and gets 
older. It is important to establish a rapport with parents and 
child while taking the history. Usually older children cooperate 
well and may sit in the examination chair alone. Younger 
children needs restrain. They feel secure and comfortable in 
parent’s lap. So, for the examination of throat the child may 
sit on a parent’s lap (see Fig. 2 in Chapter 10 “History and 
Examination—General Set-up”). Both the hands should be 
secured by the parent with one hand, while the other hand 
holds the head firmly against the chest of the parent. Children 
often get frightened seeing any instrument and would not 
cooperate. So, they should be asked to just open the mouth 
and examination may be performed without the use of 
tongue depressor. So, if need be, tongue depressor should be 
employed in last. The examination has to be quick with minimal 
discomfort to the child.

Case Study
A 50-year-old female patient has been suffering from difficulty in 
swallowing for 3 months. It is gradually progressive in nature. Initially, 
she had difficulty with solid food and had to crush the food to make 
it porridge. She feels that food stuck in the middle part of chest. 
There is no history of associated pain. Now she cannot swallow even 
porridge/soft diet and is only on plain liquid. Her dresses are getting 
loosened as she has lost weight. She has started feeling weakness 
for about 15 days. There is no history of sore throat, chest pain, 
breathlessness and fever. There is no past history of any dysphagia, 
radiation exposure, ingestion of lye. She has been smoking and 
drinking alcohol for 25 years. Surprisingly, general survey and ENT 
examination did not reveal any other pathology except anemia.

mirror is introduced into the mouth and held firmly against

For preliminary identification, bacteria are traditionally 
classified into gram-positives and gram-negatives. Cell walls of 
gram-positive bacteria are thicker and retain the color of the 
blue dye crystal violet. The gram-negative bacteria have thinner 
walls which lose the blue dye and take the color of red or pink 
safranine counterstain. Yeasts and moulds are gram-positive 
and can be identified by various other stains.

Foreign bodies of airways is a life-threatening condition and is 
the leading cause of infantile deaths and the fourth one among 
preschool children. Depending on the size and nature, a FB may 
lodge in the larynx, trachea, or bronchi. A large FB, which cannot 
pass through glottis, gets lodged in the supraglottic region. A 
small FB easily passes down into the trachea or bronchi. Sharp 
pointed FBs (such as pins, needles, or fish bones) may stick in 
either larynx or tracheobronchial tree.

Indications: Anterior nasal packing is done in cases of 
active anterior epistaxis. Cauterization of the bleeding 
area is tried first. But if bleeding is profuse and the site 
of bleeding cannot be localized, anterior nasal packing is 

done.

content.text:
Method: Nose must be cleared of blood clots by suction 
and forceps. One meter long ribbon gauze (width 2.5 cm 
in adults and 12 mm in children), which is soaked in liquid 
paraffin, is packed tightly in each nasal cavity by layering 
the gauze from floor to the roof and from before backwards. 

The initial few centimeters of ribbon gauze are folded upon 
and introduced along the floor. Some consultants prefer 
vertical layers of ribbon gauze from back to the front. If 
bleeding starts from another nose, then posterior nasal 
bleeding must be suspected. Either one or both nasal 
cavities may be packed.

reasons: bullet marker starts a list item

content.text:

2–3 days.

Critical Thinking Case and Questions
Case Study
A child of one-and-half year of age was brought to emergency/ 
casualty department with respiratory distress/stridor for 4–5 days. 
Respiratory distress was initially intermittent but now has become 
persistent. The child has been suffering with symptoms of low-
grade fever, cold and cough for 1 week. After several days of URI 
symptoms child developed hoarseness and brassy and barking 
croupy cough. The child does not have any difficulty in swallowing. 
There is no history of any foreign body (FB) ingestion or inhalation. 
Parent say that the child contracted infection from his elder brother 
who had upper respiratory infection (URI). The stridor was biphasic 
with tachycardia. Signs of upper airway obstruction (nasal flaring 
and in-drawing of suprasternal, supraclavicular, epigastric and 
intercostal spaces could be seen on clinical examination.  
See Chapter  57 “Acute and Chronic Laryngitis”.

Case Study
In monsoon season, a lady of 35 years of age came to ENT OPD with 
the complaint of right ear pain for 5 days. Now the pain has become 
so severe that she could not sleep in the last night. Along with this 
pain she is having itching and sensation of right ear fullness and 
ear block. On further inquiry she gave preceding history of self-
cleaning her right ear with ear buds. She tried some oil drops but of 
no avail. Some blackish material is coming out of the right ear. There 
is no history of associated fever, cough and cold. On examination, 
blackish debris could be seen in her right ear canal. There was no 
pain/tenderness on retracting the pinna. Rinne test was negative 
and Weber was lateralizing to diseased right ear. There was no other 
significant finding on examination.

content.text:
Millian’s ear sign: Erysipelas can spread to pinna (cuticular involvement) while cellulitis cannot as the deeper dermis 
tissue is absent here. Erysipelas and cellulitis produce erythema and warmth in absence of suppuration. Erysipelas involve 
upper dermis and cutaneous lymphatics while deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue are involved in cellulitis.

may occur on raw area. Patients need psychotherapy and antibiotics for infection. Ear packing and bandage are also

content.text:
Eczematous OE: Patient presents with intense irritation, vesicles, oozing and crusting. Hypersensitivity to microorganisms,

usually cure the disease.

Perichondritis and chondritis: Penetrating trauma—when ear piercing is done through the cartilage of the pinna and 
aseptic precautions are not maintained, this can be a common sequelae. Other etiologies include following assaults, 
animal and human bites and following ear surgery.

content.text:
Keloids: These are commonly seen after ear piercing. They present as rubbery painless nodules at the site of ear piercing 
a few months after the procedure resulting in disfigurement. Often both ears are involved and they may develop elsewhere 
in the body following surgery. They may regress with intralesional injections of steroids at weekly intervals. Otherwise 
they may need surgical excision with a suitable margin but chance of recurrence is there.

Ear maggots: Often the patients are neglected infants or old and debilitated adults with pre-existing CSOM with purulent 
foul smelling ear discharge. Multiple sittings of removal may be required because the eggs laid by the flies usually hatch 
in batches. The use of otoendoscope or microscope during removal of the maggots will help in eliminating the maggots 
in fewer sittings compared to removal by forceps with the naked eye due to better visualization.

of middle ear effusion (MEE) and features of acute infection

features of inflammation. AOM and OME represent the two 
stages of the same disorder.

epithelium-lined fistulous tract.

content.text:
The pathogenesis of acquired cholesteatoma is yet a matter of 
debate. The four basic theories are invagination, hyperplasia, 
migration and metaplasia (Fig. 8). Attempts have been made 
to explain the pathogenesis on the basis of combination of 
these theories.

reasons: block type changes (heading_candidate -> paragraph)

content.raw:
Invagination theory (Wittmaack): This theory explains 
primary acquired cholesteatoma. Invagination of tympanic 
membrane from the attic or posterosuperior part of pars 
tensa occurs in the form of retraction pockets. The outer 
surface of tympanic membrane is lined with stratified 
squamous epithelium, which after invagination, forms 
the matrix of cholesteatoma and lays down keratin in the 
pocket. 
  As the retraction pocket deepens because of negative 
middle ear pressure and repeated inflammation, desqua­
mated keratin cannot be cleared from the recess and 
results in cholesteatoma. Bacteria can infect the keratin 
matrix, forming biofilms resulting into chronic infection 
and epithelial proliferation. 
  The most common sites for this primary acquired 
cholesteatoma are pars flaccida or attic (being less fibrous 
and less resistant to displacement) and posterosuperior 
quadrant of pars tensa. The attic perforation is simply the 
proximal end of an expanding invaginated sac.

content.text:
Attic cholesteatoma first invades Prussak’s space (lateral 
most portion of epitympanum) and then into the recesses 
of epitympanum posteriorly, lateral to the body of incus. 
Inferiorly, it goes into the middle ear via pouch of von Tröltsch. 
Anteriorly, cholesteatoma enters into the protympanum. An 
attic cholesteatoma thus extends posteriorly into the aditus, 
antrum and mastoid, inferiorly into the mesotympanum and 
medially surrounds the incus and head of the malleus.

Case Study 2
A young girl of 18 years age has been suffering from left ear off and 
on discharge since her childhood. The discharge is intermittent, 
mucoid, clear or sometime yellowish and not foul smelling. When, 
she starts instilling drops in the ear, her discharge stops for months 
together. The ear starts discharging again when water goes in the ear 
while taking bath, during the episodes of cough and cold and when 
she start cleaning her ear with ear buds. She is not complaining of ear 
pain, hearing loss or tinnitus. Sometimes, she does feel that she has 
hearing difficulty but it is not her complaint. She does not have any 
associated headache and dizziness or facial weakness.

Permanent perforation: This benign type of CSOM is 
mostly the sequela of a large central perforation of child­
hood AOM, which usually follows after exanthematous 
fever. The permanent perforation allows repeated infection 
through the external ear canal causing otorrhea. The middle 
ear mucosa, which is exposed to the environment, gets 
sensitized to dust, pollen and other aeroallergens from the 
environment.

Ear discharge: The odorless ear discharge may be mucoid 
or mucopurulent, profuse or scanty and conti­nuous or 
intermittent. The ear discharge is common at the time 
of upper respiratory tract infection and when water 
enters into the ear.

Hearing loss: It is usually conductive. The severity of 
hearing loss varies but is rarely profound. The hearing 
may improve in the presence of discharge due to 

“round window shielding effect”, because the dis-

charge helps to maintain the phase differential. In the 
dry ear, sound waves reach both the oval and round 
windows simultaneously and cancel each other’s effect.

content.text:
Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from lesions of the 
cochlea, 8th nerve and central auditory pathways. There are 
characteristic features of SNHL, which differentiate it from 
conductive hearing loss (CHL) (see Chapters 13 “Hearing 
Loss—Principles of Management”). History taking and general 
management of patients with sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) 
has been discussed in Chapter 13 “Hearing Loss—Principles of 
Management”. The central auditory transmission has bilateral 
pathways from each ear. So the central defects, which cause 
subtle findings (such as impaired sound localization), are 
difficult to detect. Some of the common causes of SNHL will 
be discussed in this chapter.

Though the exact cause is not yet known, following factors have 
been implicated: hereditary predisposition, gene mutation, 
cellular ageing, chronic noise exposure, systemic diseases, 
vascular risk factors, ototoxicity, metabolism, arteriosclerosis, 
and nutritional deficiency. Poor conduction of sound impulses 
through the auditory nerve and improper interpretation at 
central auditory processing unit are important contributing 
factors to hearing loss in the elderly.

content.text:
Multiple genetic factors or potential gene groups are associated 
with presbycusis and presbystasis. Over 120 genes, which are 
related to non-syndromic deafness, had been mapped in the 
human genome but only a few of them are related to ARHL. 
More than 50% of the hearing impairment in the elderly 
is attributed to some genetic factors. About 70–80% are 
autosomal recessive and 15–25% are autosomal dominant. 
Only 1–2% are mitochondrial or X-linked genes. These genes 
are categorized into six different families: (1) transcription 
factors, (2) cytoskeleton components, (3) ion channels, (4) 
transporter, (5) extracellular matrix molecules, and (6) genes 
for stria vascularis disorders. Mutation of the mitochondrial 
genome builds up in the process of ageing and causes cochlear 
hair cell damage.

content.text:

Method: Patient is blindfolded during the test. Take two 
tuning forks of equal frequency. Vibrate and put them 
simultaneously at an equal distance (say 30 cm) from each 
ear. Patient will claim to hear it in the said normal ear. Now 
bring the tuning fork closer (say 10 cm) to the feigned ear 
(said deaf ear) while keeping the tuning fork on the normal 
side at the same distance. The patient will deny hearing in 
both ears though she must be hearing in the said normal 
ear. A patient with true hearing loss will continue to hear on

Based on anatomical structure of the nerve, Sunderland 
classified the severity of nerve injuries into five degrees. This 
classification is now widely accepted. The third, fourth and 

fifth degrees are types of neurotmesis.

content.text:
First degree (obstruction to axoplasm)—neuropraxia: 
In this conduction block, flow of axoplasm through the 
axons is obstructed. No morphological changes are seen. 

In this type of injury, recovery of function is complete. 

Nerve excitability test (NET) and maximum stimulation test 
(MST) are normal. Electromyography (EMG) fails to show 
voluntary motor action potential as they are not conducted 
across the blockade.

reasons: marker line: a marker alone on its line opens the item

content.text:
Second degree (injury to axon)—axonotmesis: There 
is loss of axons, but endoneurial tubes remain intact. 
Wallerian degeneration occurs distal to the lesion. Electrical 
tests show rapid and complete degeneration, with loss of 
voluntary motor units. During regeneration, axons will grow 
into their respective tubes. Recovery is good.

canal from the superior vestibular nerve canal.

content.text:
Facial nerve segments: Labyrinthine segment is the shortest segment (4 mm) of facial nerve. The longest segments 
(approximately 16 mm) are intracranial and parotid. Intracanalicular and tympanic are approximately 8 mm, while mastoid 
is 12 mm.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Facial nerve supplies: All the muscles derived from second branchial arch, such as muscles of facial expression and 
stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric and stapedius muscles.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Chorda tympanic nerve: This branch of facial nerve carries efferent preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers 
to submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. It joins lingual nerve in infratemporal fossa.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Greater petrosal nerve: Preganglionic secretomotor fibers for lacrimation leave the geniculate ganglion of facial nerve 
in this branch. So the tearing is lost in suprageniculate or transgeniculate lesions of facial nerve.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Parotid relations: During superficial parotidectomy, the most reliable landmark to identify main trunk of facial nerve is 
tympanomastoid suture. Other landmarks include mastoid tip, styloid process and auricular cartilage. Facial nerve exits 
anterior to digastric ridge and lies above the posterior belly of digastric.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Middle ear relations: Landmark used for identification of geniculate ganglion of facial nerve is processus cochleariformis. 
Tympanic segment of facial nerve lies above the oval window and below the horizontal semicircular canal. Mastoid segment 
of facial nerve always lies behind the tympanomastoid suture and can be located 6–8 mm deeper to tympanomastoid fissure.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Upper motor neuron facial palsy: The corticobulbar fibers unilaterally innervate the facial motor neurons of the lower face. 
Upper face has a bilateral corticobulbar innervation. Lesions of corticobulbar fibers (in brainstem and genu of internal capsule) 
result in upper motor neuron facial palsy such as in pseudobulbar palsy. Blink reflex remains intact bilaterally. Patient can 
shut both eyes with equal power and can wrinkle his forehead scalp bilaterally. Liquid drips out from the corner of mouth.

content.text:
Fitzgerald-Hallpike bithermal caloric test: The lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal is stimulated (tested) by irrigating cold 
(30°C) and warm (44°C) water in the external auditory canal. Cold water induces opposite side nystagmus while warm water 
results into the same side nystagmus [COWS (Cold, opposite; warm, same)]. In a sitting position with head tilted 60° backward, 
lateral semicircular canal is stimulated during caloric testing. To bring the lateral semicircular canal in vertical position, the 
patient’s head is raised 30° forward if s/he is in supine position but in a sitting position the head is tilted 60° backward.

content.text:
Case Study
A 25-year-old man has been suffering from nasal obstruction and 
discharge for 20 days. He says that he had an episode of acute 
common cold that lasted for 1 week but did not get cured. He tried 
different antibiotics courses of 3–4 days and nasal decongestant 
and other symptomatic treatment but of no avail. Whenever he 
feels nose block, he puts decongestant nasal drops. His severity of 
symptoms aggravated after diving and taking bath in one swimming 
pool. For the last couple of days, his symptoms are becoming more 
on right side than left. He feels some pain and fullness on right 
side of face and dental pain in the right-side upper teeth. The nasal 
discharge is thick and yellowish green and mainly on the right 
side. Now the decongestant nasal drops are not of much help. He 
has developed coughing that remains throughout the day and 
is more at night. On waking up in the morning, he has headache 
that gradually increases till mid-day and then starts subsiding 
in the evening. Anterior rhinoscopy showed congested nasal 
mucosa and marked deviated nasal septum on right side. Purulent 
exudates could be seen in middle meatus on right side. Canine 
fossa tenderness on right side of the maxillary region was observed 
on palpation. Spatula test revealed less fogging on right side.

content.text:
Case Study
A young boy of 10 years age has been suffering from nasal 
obstruction and discharge for 6 months. His parent noted some 
growth in the left nasal cavity 1 month ago. The nasal obstruction 
was initially intermittent and only on left side. Later on nasal 
obstruction became continuos and lately has involved right nose 
also. The nasal discharge though bilateral is mainly on left side. It 
is thick and yellowing green in color. His voice has become thick 
and dull with hyponasality. Anterior rhinoscopy showed left side 
soft, smooth, grayish, insensitive and mobile mass that was almost 
filling the entire left nasal cavity. Yellowish thick nasal discharge 
was present on both sides though more on left side. On probing, 
nasal mass seemed arising from the lateral wall of left nasal cavity. 
There was no bleeding while manipulating the nasal mass. Spatula 
test showed no fogging on left side and limited fogging on right 
side. Rest of the ENT examination was normal.

examination following findings were noticed: Dark and puffy lower 
eyelids, lines under the lower eyelid and transverse crease at lower 
third of nose. Anterior rhinoscopy showed: Enlarged pale-bluish 
nasal turbinates and clear or yellowish nasal discharge.

content.text:
Allergen-specific IgE antibodies are detected in serum by RAST 
or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Protein allergens 
are covalently linked to the immunosorbent (solid) phase. 
Patient’s serum is allowed to incubate with the allergen-coated 
solid phase. The system is washed, and a second incubation is 
done employing labeled anti-IgE antibody (rabbit anti-human 
IgE). The allergen-specific IgE is quantified by comparing colori­
metric changes or radioactive counts against a standard curve. 
Common allergens are available commercially for RAST or 

ELISA testing. A negative response of allergen-specific IgE is 
sufficient to rule out significant inhalant allergy.

nasal symptoms are watery discharge and stuffiness. The

uterus. The persistent congestion may lead to secondary 
infection and rhinosinusitis.

A 30-year-old lady has come to you with the complaint of nasal 
stuffiness for 1 month. Her problem started after an episode of 
mild cold for which she started using herself decongestant nasal 
drops. Whenever she feels nasal stuffiness she put nasal drops. Her 
frequency of instilling nasal drops has increased. Now she feels 
not much improvement with nasal drops. The problem of nasal 
congestion increases in night and she has to use nasal drops. She 
gets nasal stuffiness in both the nostrils that alternate from one side 
to other. In the night when she rolls on one side, the dependent 
side of nose is often blocked. She does not have any other nasal 
complaints. The lady has sedentary lifestyle and has been facing 
some office problem for 1 month. Anterior rhinoscopy examination 
showed boggy and edematous nasal mucosa. The turbinates were 
found congested and hypertrophic with clear mucoid secretions. 
The spatula test did not show any significant nasal obstruction.

Both benign and malignant tumors of the nose and paranasal 
sinuses are uncommon. The malignant neoplasms are more 
common than benign. The separation of nasal tumors from 
tumors of paranasal sinuses is difficult except in early stages. 
In addition to primary tumors, these areas can be encroached 
with growths of nasopharynx, cranial and oral cavity. The best 
approach (endoscopy versus open) depends upon various 
factors, such as tumor location, extension, size, type and 
facilities available and surgeon’s training and experience.
Benign tumors are usually smooth, localized and covered with 
mucous membrane while malignant masses are usually friable, 
have a granular/irregular surface and tend to bleed easily.

an imaginary line (OL), which extends between medial canthus 
and the angle of mandible, divides the maxilla into two regions 
anteroinferior (AI) and posterosuperior (PS). AI growths are 
easy to manage and have better prognosis than PS tumors; 
(B) Lederman’s classification. Two horizontal lines of Sebileau, 
one passing through the orbit floors (I) and other through antral 
floors (II), divide the area into three regions: Suprastructure (SS), 
Mesostructure (MS), and Infrastructure (IS). The vertical line (III) 
at the plane of medial wall of orbit separates ethmoid sinuses 
and nasal fossa from the maxillary sinuses.

Case Study
A 5 years school going boy has been suffering from throat pain 
and fever for 3 days. The problem started after couple of days of 
taking the cake, which was tasty but was not fresh. The throat pain 
is aggravated during the swallowing of food. Some times, he feels 
ear pain especially during the swallowing. The fever is high grade 
and associated with chills and rigors. Due to severe throat pain and 
fever, he could not go to school. He is giving past history of similar 
symptoms 3 to 4 times per year for the last 3–4 years. Usually, these 
episodes of sore-throat and fever begin after consuming cold drinks, 
ice creams and bakery items which he craves and enjoys the most. 
The following findings were seen on local physical examination: 
Fetid breath; Dry and coated tongue; Red and swollen tonsils with 
yellowish spots on their medial surfaces; and enlarged and tender 
upper cervical lymph nodes.

content.text:
The esophagus is subject to a variety of diseases (Box 1). The 
primary infections of the esophagus are rare except fungal 
esophagitis, which occurs in patients who are immuno­
compromised. Esophageal perforation is a surgical emergency. 
The scar formation and stricture development occur from 
ingestion of caustic agents. Foreign bodies (FBs) in esophagus 
are frequently encountered in children. The cricopharyngeal 
area is a frequent site. Benign tumors of the esophagus are 
rare. However, malignancies of the esophagus are relatively 
common.

reasons: block type changes (heading_candidate -> paragraph)

content.text:
Esophageal inflammatory disease, such as gastroesophageal 
reflux disease (GERD) is quite common. Peristaltic contractions 
of esophagus pass the food down into the stomach. The upper 
esophageal sphincter (UES) and lower esophageal sphincter 
(LES) prevent reflux of food while swallowing. Dysphagia is 
usually present in esophageal disorders. Odynophagia, painful 
swallowing indicates esophagitis.

cancer accounts for 2.63% of the whole body cancers (Indian 
Council of Medical Research). Among the most common sites 
of cancer in males, larynx was found second in Delhi Registry 
and third in Mumbai Registry. Male-to-female ratio is 10:1. 
Indians are affected more than the people of Western countries. 
Patients are mostly in the age group of 40–70 years. Tumors of 
larynx can extend to hypopharynx and vice versa. Evaluation 
of persistent hoarseness is very important in smokers and 
elderly patients.

content.text:
Incision: A postaural incision cuts through soft tissues 
and reaches up to the periosteum without cutting 
the temporalis muscle. Mastoid retractors (Jansen’s or 
Mollison’s) retract soft tissues after the postaural incision 
and elevation of flaps. The pressure on the edges of the 
incision provides hemostasis. Lempert’s endaural retractor 
is used in cases of endaural approach. Lempert’s endaural 
speculum can be used to spread open the meatus when 
giving local injection or making an endaural incision.

reasons: decimal marker starts a list item

content.text:
Exposure of mastoid: Periosteum is cut in the line of 
postaural incision. A horizontal incision is made along the 
lower border of temporalis muscle. A branch of superficial 
temporal artery is usually encountered and may need 
ligation or cauterization. Periosteum is elevated from the 
lateral surface of mastoid and posterosuperior region 
of bony meatus. Farabeuf periosteal elevator is used for 
elevation of periosteum from the mastoid cortex. Tendinous 
fibers of sternocleidomastoid muscle need sharp cutting 
near the mastoid tip. A self-retaining mastoid retractor is 
applied for the exposure.

pupils of both eyes remain dilated. But when the light is put
